newsitem.title: POLAND: World Bank lauds Poland, warns against complacency.
newsitem.headline: World Bank lauds Poland, warns against complacency.

text.p: Poland leads eastern Europe in economic reforms but it has to push ahead with structural changes to ensure steady growth needed to catch up with the European Union, a senior World Bank official said on Friday.

"There is no room for complancency...Poland's future prospects will mainly depend on the authorities' ability to implement a second round of structural reforms," the bank's representative to Poland, Paul Knotter, said.

"These reforms include social security reform, health sector reform, coal sector reform, speeding up privatisation and restructuring of troubled financial institution," Knotter told his farewell news conference.

The reform of the ailing pension system, which may udermine public finances in about eight years if left unchanged, is being discussed in parliament. It provides for creating independent pension funds and curbing pensions growth.
The government hopes the reform will be passed before the general election on September 21, because otherwise the debate of the difficult issue might start afresh.

The health care reform, which will introduce elements of the free market into the system, has already been approved and is due to take effect in 1999. But many analysts say it does not go far enough in dismantling government bureaucracy.
The government, fearing social unrest, has refrained from any radical reform of the loss-making mining industry, which is burdened with more than 10 billion zlotys in debt.

Privatisation continues but critics say it is too slow and the government lacks ideas on how to sell off heavy industrial firms, often outmoded and underfinanced, such as steel mills, chemical plants or shipyards.

Knotter said tackling these problems might prove even more difficult after the elections, in which the ruling leftist coalition of ex-communists and a peasant party could lose its current stable majority or even power.

"Any new government emerging after the forthcoming elections may face much less favourable legislative majorities and greater internal divisions than the present. This could increase rigidity in economic decision making," he said.

Knotter strongly praised Poland's growth, which reached 5.5 percent of gross domestic product in 1996 and is likely to be even higher this year, and falling inflation, with went down to 14.7 percent in May from nearly 40 percent in 1993.
But he said the government should keep the rising current account deficit under control, especially by curbing domestic consumption.
The deficit grew tenfold to $2.27 billion in the first four months of the year, compared with the same period last year, because imports growth largely surpassed exports rise.
"As of today I see no reason for concern regarding the current account deficit... At this stage of the economic growth it is normal," Knotter said.
"But the government must watch how this trend develops and take appropriate measures if neccessary," he said.
